2. The two models are not symmetric in fidelity, so this is not a taste question. That is a systematic one-directional overestimate, and it does not average out — it compounds with rung count. Over a long grind (dozens of rungs to a level cap) A prices the same real-world route materially higher than it costs. An auditor doing the obvious check — "the plan said 12 kills, the character dinged after 11" — sees the planner mispredict on the very first rung it carries over.

3. The blast radius is through the ranking, which is where it stops being cosmetic. This projection feeds the cost of a skill/level-grind route inside a unified objective that compares that route against alternatives. A uniform ~8% inflation of every grind estimate is exactly the kind of bias that flips which root the planner picks, and the wrong pick is not visibly wrong — the bot just quietly stops choosing grind routes it should have chosen. That is the failure mode that gets filed as "why is it doing X instead of levelling" rather than as an off-by-one.

4. The residuals section is silent on this. So B is a second legal reading, not a violation, and the divergence is observable in both the monster named in the rung and the total cost.

REAL gap (moderate severity; I'd score blast radius ~3/5, not 4/5). CAVEAT FIRST: no spec file path was supplied in my task, so I could not read the spec, and per the blindness constraint I did not go looking for it. This judgment assumes the witness's characterization is accurate.

Not a don't-care. The two readings disagree on BOTH fields of the emitted rung — the monster named and total_cost — and total_cost is not decoration; it is the quantity a leveling planner exists to produce and compare. An operator reading rungs = [(11, "bandit_lizard", 14)] and then observing that blue_slime crosses the same rung in 12 files exactly the bug "the planner reported a cost that was not achievable and picked the slower monster." "We maximized a per-kill ratio" is not an accepted answer when the artifact is labeled a cost to cross the rung.

The wedge is integrality of kills. The spec (as reported) publishes a per-kill reward formula and a per-kill loop_cost, which fixes the rates 70/7 = 10.0 vs 25/3 = 8.33 but is silent on the load-bearing conversion: is rung cost needed_xp / rate (continuous, ordering = per-kill argmax) or ceil(needed_xp / xp_per_kill) * loop_cost (integral, ordering can invert)? Both are faithful to every published number. That silence is the gap; A and B are its two closures.

What makes it worth fixing rather than tolerating is that the divergence is UNBOUNDED, not the 2-action toy. Ceil-rounding penalizes overshoot, and overshoot is worst exactly at a rung boundary: a monster with a superb per-kill rate but huge per-kill XP relative to remaining XP (e.g. 10000 XP at 900 actions, rate 11.1) wins the per-kill argmax, then wastes ~99% of one kill on a 100-XP remainder. Reading A selects it and charges 900 actions where a modest monster crosses in ~12. The failure mode bites hardest in the common case of finishing a nearly-complete level, and is invisible to any test that checks a single rung with a large remaining-XP gap.

Second-order, and why this is not merely "two defensible heuristics": reading A systematically OVERSTATES the achievable cost of a rung. If that number is consumed as a comparison key against other routes — the normal use of a per-rung cost — an overstating estimator is inadmissible, so a genuinely cheapest route can be silently deprioritized in favor of one whose cost happened to incur less rounding waste. That is a correctness defect in the cost model, not a preference.

Not severe in the data-loss / double-charge / tenant-leak sense: no state is corrupted, nothing is lost, both readings terminate with a legal plan. It costs wall-clock and misranks — hence below the claimed 4/5.

If the spec in fact states rung cost as ceil(needed/xp_per_kill) * loop_cost, or explicitly says selection is argmax of per-kill reward-per-cost, this is determined and my answer is a false positive. The fix either way is one clause: define rung cost in integral kills, state that selection minimizes that cost (or explicitly that it maximizes per-kill rate and may overshoot), and give a tiebreak rule for equal costs.
